title: How Much Does a Data Center BMS Cost?
summary: Typical BMS price ranges, per-point vs per-asset pricing, the line items behind seven-figure quotes, and how software-defined BMS changes the math.
body_markdown:
By[Pietro Sette](https://www.aravolta.com/blog/author/pietro-sette)


·


Aravolta


## Quick answer


For a mid-size data center, a traditional BMS project is commonly quoted in the **high six figures to low seven figures** all-in (software, controllers, panel work, programming, and commissioning) on a **six to twelve month** timeline. The spread comes from controls hardware and professional services more than from the software license. A software-defined BMS that discovers existing equipment on its own and prices **per asset instead of per point** typically lands at a fraction of that and deploys in days to weeks.


Almost nobody publishes BMS pricing, so every operator we meet asks the same two questions: what should this cost, and why was my quote so high? This guide covers where the money goes in a traditional building management system project, the pricing models vendors use, the costs that only show up after signature, and what changes when the BMS is software instead of a construction project.


## Where the money goes in a traditional BMS quote


Line item What it covers Why it gets expensive


Software licensing The head-end platform and its point count Per-point pricing scales with visibility, not value


Controllers PLCs and DDCs, panels, power supplies Proprietary hardware, long lead times


Installation labor Panel fabrication, wiring, terminations Skilled-trade hours on a live facility


Controls programming Sequences of operation coded into controllers Every change is an engineering engagement


Point-to-point commissioning Verifying every sensor and actuator end to end Manual, per-point, weeks of site time


Integration Connecting BMS to EPMS, DCIM, ticketing Cross-vendor projects with no single owner


Service contract Ongoing support, updates, emergency response Annual recurring, often 10 to 20 percent of project cost


Hardware and human hours dominate, not software. A traditional BMS is expensive because it is delivered as a construction project. That is also why quotes take weeks to produce and why the invoice grows every time the facility changes.


## Per-point vs per-asset vs flat pricing


- **Per point:** the legacy model. Every monitored value is billable. One CRAC exposes dozens of points and a modest facility carries tens of thousands. Operators respond by monitoring less than they should, which defeats the purpose of the system.
- **Per asset:** each device (CRAC, UPS, PDU, chiller) is one unit, and every metric it exposes is included. Cost tracks the size of the facility rather than how much of it you watch. This is how Aravolta prices.
- **Flat or per-kW:** simple to budget, but check what counts as in scope. “Unlimited” tiers often exclude controls, integrations, or additional sites.


When you compare quotes, normalize them to one number: total cost over three years, including the service contract and a realistic estimate of change orders. A per-point system that looks competitive on day one rarely is by year three.


## The costs that show up after signature


- **Change orders:** adding a sensor, changing a sequence, or onboarding a new device type traditionally means a controls engineer on site. In a facility that changes every month, that visit becomes a permanent budget line.
- **Point-count creep:** under per-point licensing, every new rack of equipment is a licensing event.
- **Vendor lock-in:** with a single-vendor controls stack, every expansion is a captive negotiation. Operators who buy an all-in-one hardware BMS for phase one often find phase two priced accordingly.
- **The integration you deferred:** connecting the BMS to your[EPMS](https://www.aravolta.com/epms) ,[DCIM](https://www.aravolta.com/dc-management/asset-management) , and ticketing later is its own six-figure project. Until it happens, your on-call engineer correlates incidents across consoles by hand.
- **Carrying cost:** a six to twelve month install on a revenue-generating facility is not free. Every month without monitoring is power you are not metering and overages you are not billing.


## What changes with a software-defined BMS


Most of a traditional quote pays people to tell the system what the equipment is and what to do with it. A software-defined BMS removes most of that work:


- **Automated discovery replaces mapping:** Aravolta's collector node scans the management network and identifies equipment against a library of more than 46,000 make, model, and firmware versions. Known devices come online immediately with every register and MIB already mapped. New device types are added within 48 hours at no cost.
- **Virtualized controllers replace programming visits:** supervisory logic (setpoint changes, sequencing, multi-condition responses) is configured in software with a full audit trail. Hardwired loops that have to keep running when the network is down stay on dedicated PLCs, including Aravolta's own standalone PLC hardware.
- **Existing sensors keep working:** the platform reads the BACnet, Modbus, and SNMP equipment you already own. CT clamps and IO inputs cover the rest, so on a retrofit the controls hardware line mostly disappears.
- **One platform:** BMS,[EPMS](https://www.aravolta.com/blog/epms-data-centers) ,[SCADA-style controls](https://www.aravolta.com/scada) , and DCIM share one data model, so there is no cross-system integration project to buy.


Deployment takes days instead of months, and you pay per asset instead of per point. For a fuller comparison of approaches, see[our guide to data center BMS software](https://www.aravolta.com/data-center-bms-software) and[BMS vs EPMS vs SCADA vs DCIM](https://www.aravolta.com/blog/bms-vs-epms-vs-scada-vs-dcim) .


## Seven questions to ask any BMS vendor


1. Is pricing per point or per asset, and what does my facility look like under each model at twice today's size?
2. What does a change cost after go-live: a new device, a new alarm rule, a modified sequence?
3. How long from contract to live monitoring, and what is on my critical path?
4. Does it read my existing controllers and sensors, or does the quote include replacing them?
5. Can it correlate building events with electrical and IT events, or is that a separate integration?
6. Is every metric a device exposes included, or only the points I license?
7. Can it run alongside my current BMS during a phased transition?


## Frequently asked questions


### How much does a BMS cost for a data center?


A traditional BMS project for a mid-size data center is commonly quoted in the high six figures to low seven figures once you count software licensing, controllers, panel work, integration engineering, and commissioning. Small edge or modular sites land far lower and multi-building campuses far higher. A software-defined BMS that reuses the sensors and controllers already installed usually comes in at a fraction of that, priced per asset instead of per point.


### What is per-point BMS pricing?


Per-point pricing bills you for every value the system monitors: a temperature reading, a fan status, an alarm contact. One CRAC can expose dozens of points, so a facility with a few hundred devices carries tens of thousands of billable points. The more you want to see, the more you pay.


### How long does a BMS installation take?


A traditional data center BMS install usually runs six to twelve months: controls design, panel fabrication, wiring, controller programming, point-to-point commissioning, then integration. A software-defined deployment that discovers the networked equipment already on site can be live in days and in full production in weeks.


### Can I modernize my BMS without replacing it?


Yes. The usual path is to run a newer platform alongside the existing BMS. It reads the same BACnet and Modbus devices, adds analytics, alerting, and correlation across systems, and takes over supervisory logic a piece at a time. Hardwired safety controls stay on their dedicated PLCs. You avoid a rip-and-replace on a live facility.


### Why do BMS quotes vary so much?


Scope drives the spread: greenfield or retrofit, how many points get monitored, how much control logic has to be programmed, what redundancy is required, and how much integration with EPMS, DCIM, and ticketing is included. Two quotes for the same building can differ several-fold depending on what is in and out of scope.


### Do I need a separate EPMS if I have a BMS?


In a traditional stack, yes. The BMS covers mechanical and building systems, a separate EPMS covers the electrical distribution chain, and integrating the two is its own project. A unified platform carries building systems and the electrical tree in one data model, so there is no seam to integrate.


### How does Aravolta price its BMS?

Deployment uses an on-site collector node that discovers equipment against a library of more than 46,000 make, model, and firmware versions, which removes most of the professional services line that dominates a traditional BMS quote.
